trust.heading: What Coverage Compass is, and isn't
trust.point1: Coverage Compass is an independent insurance education and comparison platform, not an insurance company, agency, or broker.
trust.point2: We provide educational information and guidance. Insurance availability and pricing vary by state, carrier, applicant, and risk.
trust.point3: Coverage Compass does not bind, cancel, or modify insurance policies.
trust.point4: Always verify final coverage details with a licensed insurance professional or insurance carrier.
trust.point5: Your document is read entirely in your browser and never uploaded to a server. Nothing is sold or shared with third parties.

q1.q: Is Coverage Compass an insurance company?
q1.a: No. Coverage Compass is an independent educational platform. We don't sell insurance, bind coverage, or represent any single carrier.

q2.q: Can Coverage Compass replace my insurance agent?
q2.a: No. Coverage Compass helps you understand your policy so your conversations with a licensed insurance professional are more productive, it's a starting point, not a substitute for licensed advice.

q3.a: Your document is read entirely in your browser and never uploaded to a server, and nothing is sold or shared with third parties. This prototype does save your review in your browser's local storage (not encrypted) so you can return to it, so avoid uploading real sensitive documents on a shared or public computer.

q4.q: What types of policies can I upload?
q4.a: Auto (personal and commercial), homeowners, renters, general liability, workers' compensation, and trucking/motor carrier policies.

q5.q: Does Coverage Compass guarantee my coverage is adequate?
q5.a: No. Coverage Compass provides educational information only. Only a licensed insurance professional can advise on and bind actual coverage decisions.

claimsHelp.heading: What to Do When You Need to File a Claim
claimsHelp.subhead: General, plain-language guidance for navigating a claim, whether it just happened or you're already in the middle of one.

step1.title: Make sure everyone is safe first
step1.body: Before anything else, get to a safe place and get medical attention if anyone is hurt. Documentation and paperwork can always wait.

step2.title: Document everything you can
step2.body: Photos and videos of the damage, the scene, and anything relevant, as soon as it's safe to take them. Write down what happened while it's fresh, dates, times, and who was involved.

step3.title: Report it to your insurance company promptly
step3.body: Most policies require "prompt" notice, and waiting too long can complicate a claim. Have your policy number and the basic facts ready when you call.

step4.title: Know your deductible before you file
step4.body: If the damage is close to or below your deductible, filing a claim may not make financial sense, ask your carrier what your out-of-pocket cost would actually be.

step5.title: Keep a record of every conversation
step5.body: Note the date, the name of who you spoke with, your claim number, and what was discussed. This matters if there's ever a disagreement about what was said.

step6.title: Understand how your payout will be calculated
step6.body: Ask whether your policy pays actual cash value (depreciated) or replacement cost, for the same damage, those numbers can be very different.

step7.title: Get a second opinion on repair estimates
step7.body: You're not required to use the first repair shop your insurer suggests. Getting an independent estimate can be worth the time on a larger claim.

step8.title: Follow up if things stall
step8.body: If your claim goes quiet, follow up in writing and ask for a status update. Most states have an insurance department that can help if a claim seems unreasonably delayed.

faq1.q: Will filing a claim raise my premium?
faq1.a: It can, especially for an at-fault claim, but it depends on your carrier, your state, and your claims history. Ask your carrier directly before you decide whether to file.

faq2.q: What if my claim gets denied?
faq2.a: Ask for the denial in writing with the specific policy language cited. You can request a re-review, involve your state insurance department, or consult an attorney for a significant claim.

faq3.q: Do I need a public adjuster?
faq3.a: For a straightforward claim, usually not. For a large or contested claim (major fire or storm damage), some people hire an independent public adjuster to negotiate on their behalf, for a fee.
